Bootstrapping: learning what a state is worth before the reward arrives

Why waiting for the final reward is slow, and how borrowing the next state's estimate lets you learn during the walk, with one worked update.

Picture a robot in a corridor of eight rooms. It always steps right, and it gets nothing until it walks out of room 8, when it gets +1. We want to know what each room is worth under that habit. The obvious approach is to walk to the end, see the +1, and hand it back to every room you passed. That is Monte Carlo prediction, and here it works fine. Now make the corridor a million steps long. Every update waits a million steps for its target. And if the robot follows a policy that never reaches an exit, there is no finished return to wait for at all.

The way out is one line of algebra. What you collect from room 3 onward is the reward for leaving room 3, plus the discounted total from room 4 onward (discounted means each extra step away counts a little less). You don't know that total yet, but you do have a guess for it. Suppose you think room 3 is worth 0.2 and room 4 is worth 0.8. You step between them and get 0. With a discount of 0.9, your new target for room 3 is 0 + 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.72. Move your old guess halfway toward that target and it becomes 0.46. That's a TD(0) update. Using your own estimate to build the target is called bootstrapping, and you can do it after every single step. You'd think that makes learning fast, and this is the part I find a little unnerving. Walk the corridor once with every guess at 0. You can update room 1 immediately, but room 2's estimate is still 0, so that wonderfully early update changes absolutely nothing.

Panel 6 is the one that bites in real training code. Keeping γ·V(s′) at a training cutoff has a name, partial-episode bootstrapping (Pardo et al., 2018). The Breaking Bellman grid game shows what a boundary mistake can look like. The robot gets 14 moves, the goal pays 1, nothing else pays, and there is no discount, so no state can be worth more than 1. One method, PPO, used learned state values and GAE to score its actions. It reached the goal only 13.3% of the time. Meanwhile, its estimate of the start state's value was about 1.44, when the most it could ever collect was 1. Bootstrapping past a real ending is a plausible way to get that number. Scoring actions with completed returns instead reached 95% (100% without subtracting V as a baseline), over 3 seeds in simulation. The success gap alone doesn't pin down a cause: the input has no clock, and a missing clock could also wreck timed behavior. No run with time left in the input has been reported, so that explanation is still open.

So here's the habit I'd take away. Whenever you build a learning target, point at three things: the rewards you actually observed, the guess you borrowed, and the place where the future stops. When a value looks wrong, the borrowed guess and that stopping place are your first two suspects. Next up is function approximation, where one network holds the guesses for every state. (Previous post: Q-learning.)

(Schulman et al., Section 3, equations 14 to 16.) Set λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 and add the discounted TD errors: each intermediate value appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign, so they cancel. On the board's example, 0 − 1 + 3 = 2, exactly the return of 4 minus the starting guess of 2. If the segment stops before the task ends, the value at that cutoff stays in the target. Smaller λ\lambdaλ gives later errors less weight, which blends in shorter horizons. People often read λ=0.95\lambda=0.95λ=0.95 as a 95%/5% mix of two estimators; it is a decay rate. Moving λ\lambdaλ trades horizons, with no guaranteed direction for variance.

# one segment, frozen V, no resets inside; r[t] is R_{t+1}
last_V = 0 if segment ended in a true terminal else V(S_H)
A = 0
for t in reversed(range(H)):
    next_V = last_V if t == H - 1 else V[t + 1]
    delta  = r[t] + gamma * next_V - V[t]
    A      = delta + gamma * lam * A
    adv[t] = A

Split the batch at every episode reset, and make SHS_HSH​ the last actual observation of the segment. Compare finish_path in Spinning Up PPO. On the board's numbers this gives 3, then 0.5, then 0.25.

Time limits: which target goes where

Pick the target at the last step from why the episode stopped:

Why it stoppedWhat it meansTarget at the last step
Real terminal (goal, crash)Nothing comes afterRRR
Training cutoff in a continuing taskThe robot would carry onR+γV(S′)R+\gamma V(S')R+γV(S′)
Real time limit in the taskTime left changes the valueRRR at the end, with time left in the state

Pardo et al.'s Last Moment task makes the third row vivid. Waiting pays 0, entering a trap pays +1, then the trap pays −1 every step until the end, so the best play is to enter on the final step. Without remaining time in the input, they report that Monte Carlo methods fail on it as well.
